screens.title: Control Flow: Making Decisions with Conditionals and Loops
screens.narratorSegment: In automation, programs need to make decisions and repeat tasks reliably. This lesson teaches you how conditional statements let a script choose actions when conditions are true or false, and how loops let a script do repeated work efficiently. You will see how comparison operators produce Boolean results that feed into conditions, how logical operators combine tests, and how for and while loops power sequence processing and retry logic. We will also cover loop controls, like break and continue, and safety checks such as correct indentation and avoiding infinite loops. Practically, you will use these tools to check service health, iterate server lists, and retry network connections until success or a retry limit is reached. By the end you will recognize when to choose a for loop versus a while loop, how to write clear if, elif, else chains, and how to guard loops so they terminate. Consider a script that checks disk usage and alerts only when a partition exceeds a threshold — that single pattern ties conditionals, comparisons, and loops together. As you learn, watch for a common misconception: indentation is not optional styling in Python, it defines the program structure. How might that change your current scripts?

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Control Flow Overview
Control Flow
Decisions and repetition are the heart of automation. Learn conditional logic and looping patterns that make scripts responsive.
In this lesson
Combine conditionals, comparisons, logical operators and loops to build reliable automation that reacts to system state.
Why it matters
Decisions and loops let scripts avoid manual repetition and handle diverse runtime situations in IT tasks like monitoring and remediation.
Explore Key Topics
Conditionals
If, elif, else chains decide actions based on True or False tests.
Comparisons & Logic
Operators produce Booleans and combine tests with and, or, not.
Loops & Controls
For and while loops repeat work; break and continue control iteration flow.
Visual concept
Cards represent rules, comparisons, and loop actions connected as a small workflow.
Condition
Check if disk usage exceeds threshold.
Outcome
Alert or continue normal processing.
Loops iterate partitions and retry network connections with a maximum attempt limit to avoid infinite loops.
Ready
Start by reviewing the learning objectives. Each screen will build practical patterns you'll apply in the hands-on activity.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will gain practical abilities that let your scripts make decisions and repeat work safely. First, you will learn to construct conditional statements using if, elif, and else so your code executes different branches when tests are true or false. This matters because automation must respond differently to healthy and unhealthy system states; for example, restarting a stopped service only when necessary. Second, you will use comparison operators like equals, not-equals, and greater-than to evaluate relationships between values, which form the basic tests inside conditionals. A third objective is to apply logical operators — and, or, not — so you can combine tests for complex conditions, such as verifying both administrative role and active status before granting access. Finally on this screen, practice implementing for loops to iterate lists, strings, and ranges to handle multiple servers or files. Each objective includes a verified competency milestone so you can demonstrate the skill with a small example script or check. Think about which objective will help your next automation task the most.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Safety and Control
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives page focuses on safe loop design and precise control. First, you will design while loops that repeat until a desired condition changes, for uses like retrying a connection. You will practice adding limits and state updates so the loop ends predictably and avoids infinite loops, a common error that wastes resources. Next, you will employ break and continue to control loop execution: break stops the loop immediately when a condition is met, while continue skips the rest of the current iteration. These statements let you search logs or skip unimportant files without extra nested logic. Another objective is to respect Python indentation as a syntactic requirement; indentation defines code blocks and incorrect spacing causes errors. Finally, you will combine these skills in a hands-on activity that simulates disk usage checks and a network retry loop, demonstrating how conditions, loops, and controls work together in a short script. Each objective links to a competency check so you can show you understand both why the construct exists and how to avoid typical mistakes.

screens.title: What is Control Flow?
screens.narratorSegment: Control flow describes the order in which statements and function calls are executed in a program. In automation, control flow decides when to take corrective action, when to skip unneeded work, and how to repeat tasks until a goal is reached. The chapter defines control flow as the sequence of statements, and it is built from three pillars: conditional statements that branch execution, comparison and logical operators that produce Boolean tests, and loops that repeat work. For example, an automated disk-check script uses a for loop to visit each partition, a comparison to test usage percent against a threshold, and a conditional to print an alert only for partitions that exceed that threshold. A common misconception is that control flow is only about loops — in practice, branching is equally important because it lets code behave differently for different system states. Misplaced indentation can also change control flow unintentionally in Python, since indentation marks suites. As you study control flow, practice writing small examples where you predict the output before running them and ask: what condition must change for this loop to stop? That habit reveals whether your flow is correct and safe.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Control flow is the program's execution order, built from conditionals, comparisons, logical operators, and loops that determine behavior in automation scripts.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › What is Control Flow?
Core idea
Control flow defines how a program chooses actions and repeats them. Branching handles alternatives; loops handle repetition.
Bullets
  • Conditionals execute blocks when a test is True.
  • Comparisons produce Boolean True/False values.
  • Logical operators combine tests for precise decisions.
  • Loops repeat actions until a condition changes or a limit is reached.
Key Takeaway

Control flow connects decisions and repetition to make automation responsive and efficient.

Example: Disk check scenario
Visual starter shows: a list of partitions iterated by a loop, each compared to a threshold, and a conditional that prints Alert, Warning, or OK based on the comparison result.
# Visual starter (conceptual)
partitions = [("C:", 75), ("D:", 90), ("/var", 82)]
for partition, usage in partitions:
    if usage > threshold:
        alert
    elif usage == threshold:
        warn
    else:
        ok
Misconception: indentation is optional — in Python, it determines the execution blocks, so keep it consistent to preserve control flow.

screens.title: If, Elif, Else: Branching with Indentation
screens.narratorSegment: Conditional statements let code choose between alternatives. An if test evaluates a Boolean expression; if it is True, the associated block runs. Elif provides another test when the first was False, and else provides a fallback when no test matches. Python uses indentation to mark each block, so consistent spacing is essential. For example, a script might check a service status string and print a message for running, stopped, or unknown states. A common beginner error is misplacing an indentation level, which either changes which statements belong to a branch or raises an IndentationError. To avoid this, use a single style — typically four spaces — and keep nested conditionals shallow where possible. A concrete example: test disk usage against a threshold and print Alert, Warning, or OK. Misconception to watch: else is not required, but if you omit it, code simply continues when no condition matches; sometimes an explicit else that logs unexpected states is safer. Try predicting the output of small if/elif/else chains before running them to validate your mental model. How would you handle an unknown service status in your monitoring script?

keyIdea.title: Branching rules
keyIdea.text: Use if for the first test, elif for subsequent tests, and else as a fallback. Maintain consistent indentation to avoid syntax errors and unintended flows.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › If / Elif / Else
What it does
Branch execution into alternative blocks depending on Boolean tests. Use elif for multiple tests and else for a final fallback.
Common mistake
Mismatched indentation that changes which lines are inside the conditional, causing logic errors or syntax exceptions.
Example outcome
Service 'running' prints a healthy message; 'stopped' triggers restart logic; unknown states are logged by else.
Code walkthrough (visual)
# Conceptual snippet shown for reading
service_status = "running"
if service_status == "running":
    print("Service is healthy.")
elif service_status == "stopped":
    print("Service is stopped. Attempting restart...")
else:
    print("Unknown service status.")
Notice how each block is defined by indentation. Omitting the else leaves unknown states unhandled, which may hide issues in automation.

screens.title: Comparison Operators
screens.narratorSegment: Comparison operators compare two values and return a Boolean result that controls conditionals. The chapter lists the common operators: equals, not equals, less than, greater than, less than or equal, and greater than or equal. In practice, you will compare numeric metrics like disk usage or C P U percentage to thresholds, or compare strings such as service status names. For example, testing whether usage is greater than a threshold returns True when an alert is needed. A frequent misconception is using a single equals when equality is intended; remember that in most languages assignment differs from equality comparison. In Python, the equals test produces a Boolean that the if statement reads to decide whether to run its block. Another practical note: comparing different types can yield unexpected results; be sure you compare numbers to numbers and strings to strings. Try checking boundary conditions — equal to threshold versus greater than threshold — to avoid off-by-one behavior. How will you check partitions that are exactly at the threshold versus those that exceed it? Comparison Operators means operators like equals, not-equals and relational comparisons return true or false and are the building blocks of conditionals.. In practical terms, use equality and relational operators to form tests.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Comparison Operators
Key operators
  • == equal to
  • != not equal to
  • <, >, <=, >= relational comparisons
Practical tip
Always ensure types match before comparing. Converting strings that represent numbers prevents surprising False outcomes.
Misconception
Confusing assignment and equality tests leads to logic errors. In conditionals, you must use the equality operator to compare values.
Concrete example
Check disk usage: if usage > threshold then alert; if usage == threshold then warn; else mark OK. This precise ordering handles boundary behavior cleanly.
Boundary check
Decide whether equal-to or greater-than triggers alert based on policy.
Type safety
Convert percent strings to numbers before comparing to avoid False results.
Key Takeaway

Choose the right comparison operator and handle equality boundaries deliberately to avoid off-by-one surprises in automation.

screens.title: Logical Operators: and, or, not
screens.narratorSegment: Logical operators let you combine multiple Boolean tests into a single condition. The chapter explains three operators: and returns True only if both operands are True; or returns True if at least one operand is True; not negates a Boolean expression. Use and when all requirements must be met, such as checking both that a user is an admin and that their account is active before granting access. Use or when alternative conditions are acceptable, for example allowing either admin status or a specific superuser name. The not operator flips a test when you want to act on the opposite case, such as running a remediation when a file does not exist. A common pitfall is misunderstanding operator precedence: and has higher precedence than or, so expressions without parentheses can evaluate differently than expected. When in doubt, add parentheses to make your intention explicit. A short exercise: rewrite a compound condition using parentheses to confirm the intended order. Closing question: which combination of operators will you use to guard access in a script that must check three separate flags? Logical Operators: and, or, not means and requires all tests to be true, or allows any true test, and not negates a test. use parentheses to avoid precedence surprises.. In practical terms, combine and negate conditions for precise decisions.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Logic rules
keyIdea.text: and requires all tests to be True, or allows any True test, and not negates a test. Use parentheses to avoid precedence surprises.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Logical Operators
Operator meanings
  • and — True if both tests are True
  • or — True if at least one test is True
  • not — flips the Boolean value
Precedence warning
and binds tighter than or. Use parentheses for clarity and to avoid logic errors.
Concrete example
Grant access only if is_admin and is_active. Use or when alternate permissions suffice, and use not to check absence like not file_exists.
Mini exercise
Consider the expression mixing or and and. Add parentheses to make the intended logic explicit and predict the outcome for different inputs. Practicing this helps avoid common precedence traps.
Use case
Allow admin access when active, or allow a specific superuser regardless of active flag.
Misconception
Assuming or and and evaluate left-to-right equally can lead to wrong branch selection.
Key Takeaway

Use logical operators to express combined conditions and parentheses to make precedence explicit and readable.

screens.title: For Loops: Iterating Sequences and Ranges
screens.narratorSegment: For loops iterate over sequences like lists, strings, tuples, and range objects to run a block once per item. In automation, use for loops to visit server lists, parse filenames, or perform repeated checks on partitions. The chapter emphasizes two common patterns: iterating directly over elements, and iterating a fixed number of times using range. For example, given a list of server names, a for loop processes each server in turn, printing a message or performing an automated action. Using range is useful when you need a specific number of attempts or to index into parallel lists. A common mistake is assuming range(N) includes N; it stops at N minus one. To avoid off-by-one errors, plan your start and stop carefully. Another tip: avoid modifying the sequence you are iterating over within the same loop, as this can skip items or cause unexpected behavior. Practice writing loops that process each partition and collect results into a new list so you keep iteration and result storage clear. How will you decide between direct iteration and using range in your scripts? For Loops: Iterating Sequences and Ranges means use for to iterate each item in a sequence, and range to generate numeric sequences. be mindful range stops before its end value.. In practical terms, process multiple items systematically using for and range.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › For Loops
When to use
Use for loops to process every item in a collection, such as all partitions or all log files returned from a directory listing.
Range note
range(stop) generates numbers 0 through stop minus one. Use start, stop, step for more control.
Common mistake
Altering the list you iterate over can skip items. Instead, build a new list of results.
Example patterns
Iterate server names to run checks. Use range when you need a specific number of attempts, like five retries.
Iterate list
for server in servers: process server
Iterate count
for i in range(5): attempt operation five times
Key Takeaway

Choose direct iteration for collections and range for counted repetitions. Watch range boundaries to avoid off-by-one errors.

screens.title: While Loops: Repeating Until a Condition Changes
screens.narratorSegment: While loops repeat a block as long as a condition remains True, making them ideal when you don't know how many iterations are needed. The chapter shows a typical retry pattern: attempt a connection, check success, and update an attempts counter so the loop ends after a maximum number of tries. The crucial safety point is to ensure the loop's condition can become False; otherwise you create an infinite loop that consumes resources. To prevent that, include a state change inside the loop or a counter that increments each iteration. A concrete example uses a connection_successful flag and attempts incremented until a max_attempts limit is reached; success breaks the loop and failure triggers a fallback after the limit. A common misconception is to assume while True loops are harmless — only use them with explicit break conditions and timeouts. Practice designing loops with clear exit conditions and consider adding logging inside each iteration to track progress. Ask yourself: what will make this while loop stop under both normal and failure conditions? While Loops: Repeating Until a Condition Changes means while repeats until false. always include state updates or counters so the loop terminates and avoid infinite loops.. In practical terms, use while for unknown iteration counts, with safeguards to prevent infinite loops.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › While Loops
When to choose while
Use while when repetition depends on a condition that changes at runtime, like waiting for a network connection to succeed.
Safety guard
Include a counter or state change inside the loop and a max attempts limit to prevent infinite loops.
Logging tip
Log each attempt to aid debugging when loops fail to exit as expected.
Example pattern
Retrying a connection up to three times: attempt, check success, set flag or increment attempts. Break early on success, or report failure after max attempts.
Failure handling
After the max attempts, perform cleanup or escalate the error instead of looping forever.
Break usage
Use break to exit immediately when the success condition is met inside the while loop.
Key Takeaway

screens.title: Break and Continue: Fine-Grained Loop Control
screens.narratorSegment: Break and continue give you targeted control inside loops. Break immediately terminates the loop and continues execution after it; continue skips the remainder of the current iteration and starts the next one. Use break when you find the item you were searching for and no longer need to process the remaining elements, which saves time and resources. Use continue to skip irrelevant items, such as temporary log files, without extra nested conditionals. A practical script example: iterate through log files, skip files ending with. tmp using continue, and stop processing entirely when a critical error file appears using break. A potential misconception is relying on continue to alter loop state unexpectedly — continue does not change the loop's index or counter unless your code does so explicitly. Also be careful that break only terminates the nearest loop; if nested loops exist you may need flags or additional logic to exit both. Practice rewriting small loops that use break and continue until you can predict the exact output for various input lists. What might you skip or stop early in your own automation tasks?

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Misconceptions
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding common mistakes helps you write more reliable automation. The most frequent errors described in the chapter are improper indentation, operator-precedence surprises with logical operators, off-by-one errors when using range, and infinite while loops without termination. Indentation in Python is syntactically significant: inconsistent spacing can change which statements belong to a conditional or loop, or raise an IndentationError. For logical operators, and has higher precedence than or; without parentheses you may get a different result than intended. With range, remember range(stop) stops before stop, which creates off-by-one problems when counting attempts. For while loops, failing to change the condition or increment a counter leads to an infinite loop that uses C P U and memory. To avoid these problems, adopt consistent indentation, add parentheses when combining logical operators, log loop iterations, and include a maximum attempt limit in retry loops. A practical habit is to mentally step through loops and branches with representative inputs before running them. What debug logs would you add to detect an infinite loop early? screens.title: Best Practices for Robust Automation
screens.narratorSegment: Robust automation combines clear control flow with logging and limits. The chapter suggests practical practices: log each iteration and key decision so you can trace behavior; use max attempts counters for retries to avoid infinite loops; keep conditionals readable with parentheses and descriptive variable names; and prefer collecting results rather than printing from deep inside loops so you can report or act on aggregated findings. When designing retries, prefer a while loop with a counter and a flag that flips on success, and add a short delay or backoff in real scripts to reduce load. For loops over a known list are straightforward, but avoid modifying the list while iterating; instead populate a new list of results. Use break sparingly to stop early on critical findings and continue to skip unimportant items. Finally, keep indentation consistent and test boundary cases like equality to thresholds and the off-by-one behavior of range. These practices make your automation scripts easier to debug, safer to run on production systems, and simpler for future maintainers. fullNarratorScript:
In automation, programs need to make decisions and repeat tasks reliably. This lesson teaches you how conditional statements let a script choose actions when conditions are true or false, and how loops let a script do repeated work efficiently. You will see how comparison operators produce Boolean results that feed into conditions, how logical operators combine tests, and how for and while loops power sequence processing and retry logic. We will also cover loop controls, like break and continue, and safety checks such as correct indentation and avoiding infinite loops. Practically, you will use these tools to check service health, iterate server lists, and retry network connections until success or a retry limit is reached. By the end you will recognize when to choose a for loop versus a while loop, how to write clear if, elif, else chains, and how to guard loops so they terminate. Consider a script that checks disk usage and alerts only when a partition exceeds a threshold — that single pattern ties conditionals, comparisons, and loops together. As you learn, watch for a common misconception: indentation is not optional styling in Python, it defines the program structure. How might that change your current scripts?

In this chapter you will gain practical abilities that let your scripts make decisions and repeat work safely. First, you will learn to construct conditional statements using if, elif, and else so your code executes different branches when tests are true or false. This matters because automation must respond differently to healthy and unhealthy system states; for example, restarting a stopped service only when necessary. Second, you will use comparison operators like equals, not-equals, and greater-than to evaluate relationships between values, which form the basic tests inside conditionals. A third objective is to apply logical operators — and, or, not — so you can combine tests for complex conditions, such as verifying both administrative role and active status before granting access. Finally on this screen, practice implementing for loops to iterate lists, strings, and ranges to handle multiple servers or files. Each objective includes a verified competency milestone so you can demonstrate the skill with a small example script or check. Think about which objective will help your next automation task the most.

This second objectives page focuses on safe loop design and precise control. First, you will design while loops that repeat until a desired condition changes, for uses like retrying a connection. You will practice adding limits and state updates so the loop ends predictably and avoids infinite loops, a common error that wastes resources. Next, you will employ break and continue to control loop execution: break stops the loop immediately when a condition is met, while continue skips the rest of the current iteration. These statements let you search logs or skip unimportant files without extra nested logic. Another objective is to respect Python indentation as a syntactic requirement; indentation defines code blocks and incorrect spacing causes errors. Finally, you will combine these skills in a hands-on activity that simulates disk usage checks and a network retry loop, demonstrating how conditions, loops, and controls work together in a short script. Each objective links to a competency check so you can show you understand both why the construct exists and how to avoid typical mistakes.

Control flow describes the order in which statements and function calls are executed in a program. In automation, control flow decides when to take corrective action, when to skip unneeded work, and how to repeat tasks until a goal is reached. The chapter defines control flow as the sequence of statements, and it is built from three pillars: conditional statements that branch execution, comparison and logical operators that produce Boolean tests, and loops that repeat work. For example, an automated disk-check script uses a for loop to visit each partition, a comparison to test usage percent against a threshold, and a conditional to print an alert only for partitions that exceed that threshold. A common misconception is that control flow is only about loops — in practice, branching is equally important because it lets code behave differently for different system states. Misplaced indentation can also change control flow unintentionally in Python, since indentation marks suites. As you study control flow, practice writing small examples where you predict the output before running them and ask: what condition must change for this loop to stop? That habit reveals whether your flow is correct and safe.

Conditional statements let code choose between alternatives. An if test evaluates a Boolean expression; if it is True, the associated block runs. Elif provides another test when the first was False, and else provides a fallback when no test matches. Python uses indentation to mark each block, so consistent spacing is essential. For example, a script might check a service status string and print a message for running, stopped, or unknown states. A common beginner error is misplacing an indentation level, which either changes which statements belong to a branch or raises an IndentationError. To avoid this, use a single style — typically four spaces — and keep nested conditionals shallow where possible. A concrete example: test disk usage against a threshold and print Alert, Warning, or OK. Misconception to watch: else is not required, but if you omit it, code simply continues when no condition matches; sometimes an explicit else that logs unexpected states is safer. Try predicting the output of small if/elif/else chains before running them to validate your mental model. How would you handle an unknown service status in your monitoring script?

Comparison operators compare two values and return a Boolean result that controls conditionals. The chapter lists the common operators: equals, not equals, less than, greater than, less than or equal, and greater than or equal. In practice, you will compare numeric metrics like disk usage or C P U percentage to thresholds, or compare strings such as service status names. For example, testing whether usage is greater than a threshold returns True when an alert is needed. A frequent misconception is using a single equals when equality is intended; remember that in most languages assignment differs from equality comparison. In Python, the equals test produces a Boolean that the if statement reads to decide whether to run its block. Another practical note: comparing different types can yield unexpected results; be sure you compare numbers to numbers and strings to strings. Try checking boundary conditions — equal to threshold versus greater than threshold — to avoid off-by-one behavior. How will you check partitions that are exactly at the threshold versus those that exceed it? In practical terms, use equality and relational operators to form tests.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Logical operators let you combine multiple Boolean tests into a single condition. The chapter explains three operators: and returns True only if both operands are True; or returns True if at least one operand is True; not negates a Boolean expression. Use and when all requirements must be met, such as checking both that a user is an admin and that their account is active before granting access. Use or when alternative conditions are acceptable, for example allowing either admin status or a specific superuser name. The not operator flips a test when you want to act on the opposite case, such as running a remediation when a file does not exist. A common pitfall is misunderstanding operator precedence: and has higher precedence than or, so expressions without parentheses can evaluate differently than expected. When in doubt, add parentheses to make your intention explicit. A short exercise: rewrite a compound condition using parentheses to confirm the intended order. For loops iterate over sequences like lists, strings, tuples, and range objects to run a block once per item. In automation, use for loops to visit server lists, parse filenames, or perform repeated checks on partitions. The chapter emphasizes two common patterns: iterating directly over elements, and iterating a fixed number of times using range. For example, given a list of server names, a for loop processes each server in turn, printing a message or performing an automated action. Using range is useful when you need a specific number of attempts or to index into parallel lists. A common mistake is assuming range(N) includes N; it stops at N minus one. To avoid off-by-one errors, plan your start and stop carefully. Another tip: avoid modifying the sequence you are iterating over within the same loop, as this can skip items or cause unexpected behavior. While loops repeat a block as long as a condition remains True, making them ideal when you don't know how many iterations are needed. The chapter shows a typical retry pattern: attempt a connection, check success, and update an attempts counter so the loop ends after a maximum number of tries. The crucial safety point is to ensure the loop's condition can become False; otherwise you create an infinite loop that consumes resources.
